data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is fully defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, pragmatic decision rule based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness) rather than probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' cannot be defined without relying on inductive assumptions about the structure of reality.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the act of preferring one theory over another implicitly assumes that past success predicts future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If no non-probabilistic metric can distinguish between two unfalsified theories other than arbitrary choice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical probability of a theory (which remains zero or undefined for universal laws) and its empirical content. A theory that survives severe tests has demonstrated high empirical content and resilience. Choosing it is not an inference that it is 'true' or 'probable,' but a rational wager that the theory with higher verisimilitude is closer to the truth. The mechanism is 'critical preference': we prefer the theory that has withstood our best attempts to falsify it, not because the future will resemble the past (induction), but because it is the only one currently standing as a viable candidate for truth.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
